entities.name: Emperor Shang of Tang
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Emperor Shang of Tang (Li Chongmao, r. 710 CE), also known by his posthumous title Emperor Shao, reigned for a mere two months over the vast Tang Dynasty of China, a period of profound political instability following the collapse of Empress Wu Zetian's interregnum. His brief, largely nominal rule from the imperial capital of Chang'an marked a critical juncture in the succession struggles that plagued the early 8th century, serving as a pawn in the power plays between his mother, Empress Dowager Wei, and his aunt, Princess Taiping. Though his personal influence was negligible, his ascension and rapid deposition highlight the ruthless machinations within the imperial court that shaped the future trajectory of one of China's most illustrious dynasties.

Li Chongmao's ephemeral reign began on July 8, 710, when his mother, Empress Dowager Wei, orchestrated the poisoning of his father, Emperor Zhongzong, to consolidate her own power. As the youngest son, Li Chongmao, then only sixteen years old, was placed on the throne as a puppet ruler, with Empress Dowager Wei assuming the role of regent and effectively controlling the government. Her ambition mirrored that of Wu Zetian, as she began to install her relatives in key positions and contemplated usurping the throne herself. This naked power grab, however, provoked a swift and violent reaction from other factions within the imperial family, particularly Princess Taiping and Li Longji (the future Emperor Xuanzong), who recognized the existential threat to the Li imperial lineage.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Emperor Shang's brief, puppet reign was a pivotal moment in the Tang Dynasty's succession crises, directly precipitating the 'Tang Long Coup' which solidified the power of future Emperor Xuanzong. His deposition marked the end of Empress Dowager Wei's ambitious regency and cleared the path for the Kaiyuan Golden Age.
